title: Merge K Sorted Lists
description: Merge k sorted linked lists into one using a min-heap of the current heads, or pairwise divide-and-conquer.

data.text: You are given an array of `k` linked lists, each sorted in ascending order. Merge them into one sorted linked list and return its head.
Approach 1: Merge One at a Time
Repeatedly merge the accumulated result with the next list. Each merge re-walks the entire result, so a long first list is re-read k times: O(k² · n) in the worst case.

data.title: Sequential merge — O(k² · n) worst case
data.content: Reuses the two-list merge k-1 times.

data.text: At any moment, the next output node must be the smallest of the k current heads. Put all heads in a min-heap, repeatedly pop the smallest, append it, and push its successor. Each of the n total nodes costs O(log k).

data.title: Min-heap — O(n log k)
data.content: The heap always contains exactly one node per non-empty list.

data.title: Use a dummy head node
data.text: A sentinel `dummy` node removes the special case for 'what is the first node' and makes the append loop uniform. Always remember to return `dummy.next`, not `dummy`.

data.title: Beware value ties in the heap
data.text: `PriorityQueue` breaks ties unpredictably when two nodes share a priority. That is fine here because ties produce any valid sorted order, but if you needed a stable merge you would compare by (value, list index).
Pair up the lists and merge each pair, halving the list count on every round. This avoids the heap entirely and achieves the same O(n log k) with less memory overhead.

data.title: Pairwise merge — O(n log k), no heap
data.content: log k rounds, each visiting n nodes.

data.caption: The heap holds one head per list; the smallest head becomes the next output node and is replaced by its successor.

data.title: Complete solution
data.content: The heap approach generalises to merging any number of sorted *streams*, which is the real-world use case: log aggregation, sorted file merges, and external merge sort all use exactly this pattern.
